name: Wage Line
one_liner: Pins every federally funded job to the exact wage-determination revision in force, then generates the week's WH-347 and state e-CPR XML from a payroll CSV — so the rate on the certified payroll is the rate the auditor will look up.
summary: JTBD (Christensen): not "buy payroll software" but "get Friday's certified payroll out the door with rates I can defend." Every contractor on federally funded work over $2,000 files a weekly WH-347 with a signed compliance statement; a single form carries ~168 discrete data points per worker and DOL-derived estimates put manual completion at over an hour per employee per report — 15+ hours a week for a 15-person crew, ~$19,500/yr on one project. Beachhead (Moore): open-shop specialty subs with 5–75 field employees, launched into California public works first (DIR eCPR is a mandatory weekly XML upload and it is the largest public-works market in the US), then federal WH-347 nationally, then NY/WA/NJ/IL. WTP (Ramanujam): price against the avoided loss, not the seat — DBA civil penalties run to $28,619 per violation plus back wages with interest, three-year debarment and False Claims Act treble damages on each false submission, and WHD recovered $259M in FY2025. Incumbents (LCPtracker, eBacon, Points North, eMars, Elation) are demo-and-quote at $175–$1,200/mo with $995–$4,995 setup fees, so zero setup fee is itself the wedge; contractors describe LCPtracker exports as "revision hell." Moat (Helmer, cornered resource): SAM.gov publishes no bulk wage-determination download, so a mirrored full revision history with per-classification diffs is assembly nobody else has — compounded by a proprietary payroll-title → SOC → WD-class → fringe-treatment crosswalk grown from every filing generated and every user correction, which no incumbent has because they make the contractor pick the class by hand. Bullseye (Weinberg & Mares): free public county×craft rate-lookup pages and a free single WH-347 generator, ranking on long-tail "[county] [craft] prevailing wage rate" against essentially no structured competition; SAM.gov/USASpending award feeds identify subs who just won DBA-covered work, so the cold list generates itself. Positioning (Dunford): not a payroll system and not a portal — the rate-of-record and artifact engine that feeds whatever portal the GC mandates. Scope honestly to open-shop/cash-fringe contractors in v1, since union CBA fringe schedules are not in public WDs.
autonomy_case: A1: email + card, five-field project setup (county, construction type, WD number or find-it-for-me, funding source), first WH-347 inside one session; a $49 one-time bid rate card is purchasable before an account exists. A2: the arithmetic — gross, fringe credit, cash-in-lieu, CWHSSA overtime, deductions — is plain deterministic code, never a model; the PDF and the XSD-validated XML are emitted directly, no review queue and no turnaround window. The model touches only classification mapping and exception-report narrative. A3: the honest failure is a crew trade matching no WD classification. The engine refuses to guess — it shows the top three candidate classifications with verbatim scope-of-work text and rate for each, blocks that payroll line from generation, and writes the user's choice into per-account classification memory so it never asks twice. A superseded WD or unresolvable county/date yields a "DRAFT — NOT CERTIFIABLE" watermark with the signature block withheld. On FAR 22.404-6 timing it states the rule and the observable dates ("Mod 14 published 6 days before bid opening") and explicitly declines to conclude effectiveness, because that turns on a contracting-officer finding it cannot see. It describes the SF-1444 conformance path and says plainly it will not file it. No contact-support path exists in the compliance flow. A4: SAM.gov's determination index returns JSON carrying revisionNumber, modifiedDate, isActive, constructionTypes and county rows per record (4,236 active DBA determinations verified live), crawled nightly and diffed per WD; CA DIR pinned to the Feb 22 / Aug 22 cycle; eCFR Parts 1, 3 and 5 diffed Mondays. Every report footers the WD number, modification date and corpus version, and a report generated against a since-modified WD surfaces a one-click regenerate. A5: the XSD hash check fails closed — a schema change blocks XML generation entirely and shows the diff rather than silently emitting a rejectable file; an index run returning materially fewer records than the last good run halts as suspected truncation; if SAM is unreachable at generation time the report is blocked rather than built on a possibly-stale rate. A6: zero human minutes — the only human-shaped question ("which class is this guy?") is answered by the in-product candidate picker.

name: Sunset Graph
one_liner: Joins every vendor's dated deprecation and breaking-change record to the exact call sites in your repos, and ships the countdown plus a test-gated migration PR before the sunset.
summary: JTBD (Christensen): "tell me what breaks, when, and where in my code, so I can put it in this sprint instead of next quarter's fire." Renovate and Dependabot bump the version number and leave the changelog archaeology to you; practitioners on HN state it directly — "you need to read the changelog to figure out if there's a breaking change, you don't trust semver" — and Infield's founder names the worst class as "changes that are missing from the changelog." Beachhead (Moore): Shopify and marketplace app vendors and 2–30 engineer agencies whose revenue depends on one connector staying alive, because the penalty there is automatic and existential rather than annoying — Shopify supports an API version for a minimum of 12 months and delists apps still calling unsupported resources, blocking installs for at least seven days; Amazon states plainly that "calls to deprecated resources will fail beginning on their sunset date" and is removing Catalog Items v0 for sellers effective 2026-03-31. WTP (Ramanujam, Hormozi): price against the avoided loss, not the crawl — one engineer-day of changelog archaeology per quarter at ~$700 loaded already covers the Team tier, and the downside prevented is store delisting, not inconvenience. Moat (Helmer + Thiel's honest test): the PR-opening mechanics take a weekend, so the defensible asset must be the breaking-change atom corpus, produced by two independent producers — LLM extraction from CHANGELOG/UPGRADING/migration docs, and mechanical public-API surface diffs computed by downloading both published artifacts and diffing exported symbols and type signatures (TypeScript declarations, Python AST, Ruby method tables, Java class files). Atoms confirmed by both are HIGH; surface-diff-only atoms are flagged "undocumented breaking change," which is precisely the class practitioners say hurts most and which nothing on the market surfaces. Layered on top is the dated event history, which cannot be backfilled: you cannot retroactively buy what Stripe's changelog said on 2026-03-14. Bullseye (Weinberg & Mares, Ries): a free public per-platform sunset calendar that ranks for the literal query "is X deprecated Shopify 2026," a GitHub Marketplace listing, and a free single-repo scan that returns a real count of at-risk call sites before asking for payment — the free scan is the experiment that measures whether the pain is real. Start with the ~200 packages causing 80% of the pain rather than chasing coverage.
autonomy_case: A1: GitHub App install → repo select → scan → Stripe Checkout, all in-browser, first impact report after the first lockfile parse. A2: the mapping is deterministic — tree-sitter parse, import/call-graph, lockfile and IaC parse; the LLM only normalizes changelog prose into the event schema and drafts migration notes, both JSON-schema-validated and rejected on failure. Draft PRs open automatically with the impact report and spec citation in the body; the customer's own CI is the adjudicator, so code review happens in their pipeline and never in a queue we staff. A3: this is the strongest low-confidence story in the pool because schema diffs are ground truth — the model does not opine on whether something is deprecated, it reads it, and every claim anchors to a concrete symbol in a concrete spec at a concrete version. Where a platform removed a field with no published replacement, or the call site is dynamically constructed, it degrades to "Detected usage, replacement unknown" with source_url and the exact call site and explicitly does NOT open a PR. Low-confidence atoms never get a codemod and are listed under "check these by hand" with the source span. If fewer than a threshold share of a package's atoms are HIGH, it declines to open a PR at all and ships report-only, stating why. Coverage is measured and reported ("we parsed 91% of call sites; 34 dynamic sites unresolved") rather than implying completeness, and a package whose latest release has not been analysed shows as "not yet analysed" rather than "no breaking changes." A4: every source is a stable machine-readable artifact rather than a fragile scrape — Shopify GraphQL SDL per version, Stripe's public OpenAPI spec, SP-API OpenAPI models, endoflife.date /api/v1 (464 products), Azure Release Communications RSS, GKE deprecation tables, the Kubernetes deprecated-API migration guide, and npm/PyPI/RubyGems/Maven release firehoses polled every 15 minutes. A5: nightly spec pulls plus per-repo rescan on push webhook; a batch failing schema validation is discarded and the previous good snapshot stays authoritative; a failed spec pull freezes that platform's countdowns and surfaces the freeze rather than serving stale sunset dates; codemods run in a sandbox and must leave the test suite at least as green as before or no PR opens. A6: zero human minutes — the PR body always carries its own evidence, so the modal question answers itself.

name: Ship Record
one_liner: Turns your per-release SBOM and your vendor list into the dated evidence artifacts procurement and regulators actually ask for — attribution NOTICE, licence-change and subprocessor alerts, and the CRA 24-hour exploited-vulnerability clock.
summary: JTBD (Christensen): "let me survive enterprise legal review and the 24-hour clock without hiring anyone" — not "give me a vulnerability scanner." One person owns all three surfaces: the CTO or founding engineer at a 10–200 person software/IoT vendor who just got the attribution request in a procurement thread, the CRA question from a board member, and the security questionnaire. Beachhead (Moore): EU-selling software, IoT, embedded and devtool vendors with no security team, timed to a live deadline — from 11 September 2026, four weeks out, manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities to ENISA within 24 hours with a full notification at 72, scope includes software shipped before that date, and penalties run to EUR 15M or 2.5% of worldwide turnover. Because SBOM obligations are not formally enforceable until December 2027, the 24-hour clock creates an implicit 15-month-early SBOM deadline: you cannot report what you cannot see, and a 24-hour clock leaves no room for manual component archaeology. The second surface is continuous and boring: everything you ship that leaves your servers owes attribution, and licences change underneath you — Redis moved BSD-3 to RSALv2/SSPL at 7.4, Terraform MPL to BSL, Elasticsearch to SSPL. The third is GDPR Art. 28(2), where the market-standard subprocessor objection window is ~15 days, so "if a vendor gives thirty days to object and you check quarterly, the cadence has silently waived the right." WTP (Ramanujam): the price ladder is bracketed by real self-serve comparables — FOSSA at ~$207/mo for ten projects, sbomify at $159/mo, PageCrawl at $13–83/mo proving people already pay for scheduled page monitoring with zero domain intelligence — and the packaging boundary sits where the value step is: does it produce the filing artifact. Moat (Helmer, pure time-locked cornered resource, three layers): per-release SBOMs a competitor cannot recreate retroactively; per-package dated licence-declaration history (you cannot retro-acquire what a package's LICENSE said on a date); and dated vendor governance-surface snapshots. On top sits the obligation matrix we author — SPDX ID × distribution mode → which duties trigger — because SPDX gives you licence identity for free and nobody gives you the obligation encoding. Unit economics improve with scale: one fetch of a vendor's subprocessor page serves every customer watching it. Bullseye: free NOTICE-file scanner for any public GitHub repo, free subprocessor change feed for the top 200 SaaS and AI vendors, free deterministic CRA scope checker as the deadline capture — all SEO-native and link-earning.
autonomy_case: A1: GitHub App plus Stripe Checkout, first SBOM within one CI run and first watch under three minutes; vendors are picked from a catalogue or pasted as URLs. A2: licence detection is deterministic text hashing and template matching against SPDX licence texts; NOTICE assembly is templated from the obligation matrix; clock arithmetic and notification assembly are code. The LLM writes only narrative fields into a fixed template with facts injected, and a validator then checks every required ENISA field is present; an unrecognised licence summarised by the model is always displayed alongside the raw text. A3: a fuzzy component-name match to a KEV entry is never clock-starting — it renders "Possible match, not clock-starting" with both records side by side and a one-click this-is/is-not that writes to the customer's own VEX suppression list, narrowing future claims. Unidentifiable licences go to a visible "Unresolved — N components" bucket, are excluded from any completeness claim, and the emitted artifact carries an explicit dated caveat listing them; the product refuses to stamp a clean bill it cannot support. An unclassifiable vendor diff emits "Unclassified change" showing the raw before/after with no risk score and asserts no obligation. A page behind a login or bot wall shows "cannot observe — vendor blocks automated access" with the date, and offers a one-click forwarding address so the vendor's own notice emails are parsed instead. The product states permanently and in-product that it detects and drafts but does not file, and is not legal advice. No queue, no expert, no escalation. A4: SPDX license-list-data (v3.28.0, dated 2026-02-20, versioned per release), CISA KEV, OSV.dev v1, GHSA, EPSS, registry metadata plus LICENSE hashes nightly at 02:00 UTC, EU/ENISA guidance diffed weekly into a versioned obligation-model changelog, and vendor surfaces tiered 6h/daily/weekly with new customer requests entering the crawl within 15 minutes. A5: silence is never rendered as safety — three consecutive fetch failures flip a surface to UNWATCHED with a dated banner; if SBOM generation fails for a release the last good SBOM stays authoritative and the new version is marked UNWATCHED loudly; KEV unrefreshed for 36h degrades the product to OSV-only mode with explicitly narrowed claims; a stale source auto-credits the next invoice through the Stripe API. A6: zero human minutes — the obligation matrix itself is published and browsable, and each event shows the raw source span that produced it.

name: Portfolio Guard
one_liner: Read-only into every client account an agency runs — ad accounts, app listings, WordPress sites, sending domains — mapping each platform's dated published rule change onto the specific entities in each client it will break.
summary: JTBD (Christensen): "don't let me be the one who finds out on Monday." The unit of pain is the portfolio, not the account — one policy sweep hits every client simultaneously and the agency eats the blame, which is exactly why per-portfolio pricing beats per-account pricing and why no single platform will ever build this (Google will never cover Microsoft, Meta and Apple in one countdown). Beachhead (Moore): performance agencies in policy-hot verticals (healthcare/supplements, finance, legal, prediction markets, crypto) managing $25k–$500k/mo across 5–75 accounts, where Google's own dated batches — Prediction Markets 2026-01-21, Limited Ad Serving expansion June 2026, Local Services 2026-07-06 — land on every client at once, delivery silently goes to zero, and Google's docs confirm a disapproved item "won't be able to run until the policy violation is fixed and the ad is reviewed again." This is Graham's live-in-the-future logic: the effective date is already published, the tooling to act before it lands is not. WTP (Ramanujam): the value metric is connected accounts and managed spend, both metered automatically from the API, so expansion happens without a salesperson; anchored on published comparables — Opteo at $129/$249/$499 for 10/25/75 accounts, Optmyzr from ~$208/mo, WP Remote at $19.99/site (40 sites = $800/mo versus $149 per portfolio) — none of which sell policy-change impact. Moat (Helmer): the diff history is cumulative and cannot be backfilled once Google overwrites a page, and on top of it sits the join table from policy clause to observable account fact (Contacts Permissions policy → READ_CONTACTS in manifest without Contact Picker usage), built once per clause and reused across every customer forever. Bullseye (Weinberg & Mares): a free weekly Policy Delta Digest of every ad-platform change with effective dates — genuinely useful standalone, ranks for the exact policy names advertisers search the day after a disapproval, and is itself the product demo. Positioning (Dunford): against "we find out when it breaks," not against other monitors. Honest sequencing caveat: the four surfaces share one portfolio spine but four different corpora, so launch on ad policy (sharpest money link — spend stops) and treat Play/App Store deadlines, WordPress plugin constraints and Postmaster deliverability as validated adjacent surfaces, not a simultaneous v1.
autonomy_case: A1: OAuth and Stripe Checkout on the same screen, first impact report within ~90 seconds of token grant; the App Store Connect key and Play service account are self-issued by the customer in their own console, and DNS verification plus Postmaster OAuth need no involvement from us. A2: the deliverable is a generated impact report and per-entity remediation list from the diff pipeline plus a retrieval-grounded matcher — every claim emitted with the exact policy paragraph and URL it came from (Lewis et al. 2020 RAG: retrieve and cite rather than recall). A3: confidence is a first-class output, tiered by evidence strength. "Confirmed" is a directly observable fact (target SDK 33 against a 31 August 2026 requirement is arithmetic, not judgement). "Possible" names the fact it cannot see — "we can see you declare READ_CONTACTS; we cannot see whether you use the Contact Picker" — and asks a single in-product yes/no the developer answers themselves, which is self-service, not escalation. "Not applicable" is stated with the reason. Where there is no evidence either way for a plugin pair, it says so rather than inventing a conflict, and the safe-apply order degrades to "apply nothing today, these three are unverifiable." Findings carry provenance tiers — declared (hard metadata fields), changelog-stated (quoted verbatim), community-reported (source thread shown, lower confidence band). A domain below Postmaster's reporting volume floor is marked "blind: below Gmail's reporting threshold," never a green check, because "no data" and "no problem" must never look identical. Zero-match runs report "no affected entities found" with the entity count scanned. Users dismiss flags, which trains the account threshold. No ticket queue, no "our team will review," no contacting a plugin author. A4: policy sitemaps with conditional-GET hourly, daily 02:00 UTC content-hash diff, weekly full re-crawl for pages that change without sitemap updates; Play's Policy Deadlines table is already tabular with deadline/policy/resources columns; the WordPress.org plugins API returns per-plugin JSON with requires, tested, requires_php, last_updated and full version history; Postmaster v2 reached GA 3 Feb 2026 with batchQuery and compliance-status endpoints. A5: every source carries last_seen_200 and last_hash_change; past 72–96h the policy family is marked "unverified since <date>" and new claims sourced from it are suppressed; a crawler that cannot verify freshness skips the account rescan and shows the stale banner rather than emitting a stale verdict; a failed pull marks the domain degraded to the customer's own alert channel rather than continuing to report healthy; a known-good fixture must reproduce its known-good report before any new index is promoted. A6: the only stateful thing per customer is an OAuth token, and expiry is handled by an in-product reconnect prompt rather than an email to a human.

name: Rate Card
one_liner: Recomputes the bills your vendors send against the rate cards those same vendors publish — parcel, card processing, delivery-platform payouts — on a flat fee, so you keep 100% of anything you recover.
summary: JTBD (Christensen): "know my number." Each of these bills is a deterministic function of a public rate card the payer never checks. Positioning (Dunford — the sharpest line in the pool): explicitly not contingency. LateShipment's OneAudit takes 25–35% of refunds recovered and by construction only touches refundable errors, leaving the larger non-refundable mispricing (fuel mis-rate, wrong zone, DIM error, residential misclassification) untouched because it produces no refund to skim; Swipesum, FeeQuery and merchantstatementaudit.com give away "free statement analysis" as processor-switch lead-gen, so their diagnosis is structurally biased. Flat fee, no recovery share, no referral revenue, no processor recommendation IS the product. Beachhead (Moore; Christensen low-end disruption): ecommerce/DTC and B2B shippers at $5k–$150k/month parcel spend and merchants at $500k–$20M/yr card volume — deliberately below the floor where Sifted, Reveel, TransImpact and Shipware bother to quote ("shippers get the most value at $200,000+ in annual parcel volume"), and below where contingency consultants are adversely selected toward large accounts. WTP: the buyer can do the math in their head. The 2026 GRI headline was 5.9% but accessorials rose 5.5–6.0% on top and new DIM/cubic criteria push real cost increases to 8–12%; up to 5% of parcel invoices contain costly errors; address correction is $25.50; typical interchange leakage runs $200–$600/mo with 50–100bp recoverable on commercial cards; Visa's CEDP change on 24 Jan 2026 inverted the incentive so merchants sending unverified enhanced data now pay MORE than those sending none. $149 flat beats $180 of contingency on a $600 recovery and also covers the bucket contingency ignores. Moat (Helmer): the effective-dated rulebook — you cannot correctly reprice a June invoice with August's fuel table, and nobody sells that time series below enterprise — compounded by a parsed statement-geometry and fee-code taxonomy per processor family and per platform report version, which is assembled once and grows with every statement processed. Bullseye (Weinberg & Mares): a free "will my box get hit by the new cubic rule?" calculator — enter L×W×H and weight, get an instant yes/no with the exact threshold and effective date cited. It ranks for the panic query, is useful in ten seconds, and the natural next question ("how many of my SKUs?") is the paid product. Sequencing: parcel first, because it has the best A4 (EIA publishes weekly, FedEx ships rate and DAS/PAS files as XLS not just PDF) and the cleanest ingestion path (the customer downloads their own UPS Billing Data or FedEx Billing Online file, so there is no carrier-credential sharing and no scraping ToS exposure); then card interchange; then delivery-platform payouts, where the 14/30/30-day dispute windows add a genuine clock.
autonomy_case: A1: upload the billing export you already own or connect read-only, Stripe Checkout, report in minutes — in direct contrast to every incumbent's quote form; a $149 one-shot teardown is the self-serve entry that converts to monitoring. A2: no LLM sits in the money path at all. The recompute is deterministic arithmetic against effective-dated tables; the model only normalizes unfamiliar invoice column headers and statement layouts, and its output is schema-validated before use. A3: the honest limits are named rather than papered over. Negotiated discounts are private, so results default to "published-rate basis" with every figure labelled as such, switching to "contract basis" only when the customer enters their schedule — and the engine learns each customer's effective discount from their own invoice history and audits consistency, since a discount that silently changes mid-contract is itself a high-value finding. A shipment whose ship date falls outside every ingested tariff version is quarantined as "Not priced — no published tariff ingested for <date>" and EXCLUDED from the savings total rather than estimated. A fee code matching no known published program lands in an explicit "Unattributed charges" bucket showing the raw statement text and amount, never a guess. Where invoiced and computed diverge and the gap cannot be attributed to a known rule, it reports "unexplained variance: $X on N shipments" as its own line rather than inventing a cause. Guarantee eligibility is asserted only where a published commitment time exists for that service, lane and date. Where a platform's published rate page cannot be verified within 7 days, it falls back to the customer's own trailing-90-day observed effective rate and labels every comparison "observed baseline — published rate unverified as of <date>" rather than asserting a violation. Headline savings are always a floor, never a guess. If priced coverage falls below 80% of invoice lines, or parse confidence fails on more than 10% of items, the run is marked Partial, the leakage estimate is SUPPRESSED rather than fabricated, and Stripe auto-credits or refunds without a ticket. Dispute documents are drafted and deep-linked into the merchant portal, but the customer clicks submit — we never act as agent. A4: the EIA weekly diesel and jet-fuel series is a free public API published Mondays and doubles as an independent check on the carrier's own banding; carrier rate and DAS/PAS ZIP files are content-hashed nightly in XLS; Visa and Mastercard schedules run an April/October cadence with hard 15 April and 15 October checkpoints; platform pricing pages are hash-diffed daily with a stored screenshot as evidence. A5: a failed rulebook pull fails closed and freezes new verdicts; if no new schedule lands within 7 days of the expected publication window the app banners "rate tables may be stale as of <date>" and suppresses drift conclusions; a golden canary invoice and statement are re-scored nightly against expected output and divergence blocks the deploy pipeline. A6: zero human minutes — support is bounded to CSV column mapping, handled by an in-product mapper with a downloadable template and an auto-generated fee-code glossary so the most common question answers itself.

name: Landed
one_liner: Classifies your catalog to 10-digit HTS with the CBP rulings behind each code, prices the full stacked duty, and — the part nobody covers — models the retroactive AD/CVD liability that lands eighteen months after a zero cash deposit.
summary: JTBD (Christensen): "will this entry cost what I think it costs, and what am I not reserving for." Since 29 August 2025 every commercial shipment into the US needs a formal entry with a 10-digit HTS code and full duty regardless of value or origin, with de minimis suspension moved into permanent regulation on 24 June 2026 and statutory repeal following 1 July 2027 — so hundreds of thousands of sellers who never touched customs now owe reasonable care. But classification is deliberately not the wedge, because that is the crowded end: Gaia Dynamics, 3CE, Zonos Classify and the hclassify Shopify app already sell AI HTS classification, several fully self-serve. The wedge is the expensive half nobody covers. An importer "can post a zero percent AD/CVD cash deposit on an entry and still owe six figures eighteen months later, once Commerce finishes reviewing the rate," with final margins running from a few percent to several hundred percent of value plus separate 19 U.S.C. 1592 penalties if CBP opens an EAPA evasion case. A zero deposit does not mean out of scope — it means the last calculated rate for that exporter happened to be zero — and most small importers check once, reserve nothing, and never track the administrative-review anniversary calendar. A 2026 competitive review of trade-alert services finds the free options unusable ("the volume is unmanageable... filtering happens entirely on your side" for the Federal Register; CSMS "assumes reader knows which messages apply to their codes"; "keyword match is not catalog match") and that same review does not address AD/CVD or scope rulings at all. Beachhead (Moore): importers of record at $2M–$150M landed value in AD/CVD-exposed goods — steel and aluminium derivatives, fasteners, cabinets and vanities, quartz, solar, tyres, wire and cable, mattresses — specifically the controller, ops lead or owner who signs the customs bond. WTP (Ramanujam): one unanticipated six-figure liquidation bill makes $899/mo a rounding error, so price to the avoided loss rather than to Tariff Sentinel's free research preview. Moat (Helmer): the join nobody has — a normalized graph of order → case → exporter → rate → effective period → scope holdings keyed to HTS × origin, with every historical rate retained so retroactive liability is computable rather than guessed, plus a structured index of scope-ruling holdings by product description that exists in usable form nowhere. Channel: customs brokers give informal versions away as relationship glue, so a broker seat tier with client workspaces deliberately makes them the channel rather than the competitor; plus free public duty-lookup pages per HTS code and origin, because importers search their own codes. Structural tailwind: AD/CVD orders and administrative reviews run on a statutory calendar regardless of the political weather, which is exactly why the wedge is AD/CVD and not headline tariffs.
autonomy_case: A1: email plus Stripe, no brokerage login, no demo; the $299 exposure snapshot is a file upload and a checkout, and the catalog side lists on the Shopify App Store with the first 5 SKUs classified free as the paywall hook. A2: classification is a retrieval-and-rank pipeline over HTS plus CROSS with the duty stack computed deterministically from the rate tables; the alerts, duty-delta math, administrative-review calendar and exposure PDF are all generated from the graph; nothing is reviewed by a person. A3: the engine never asserts scope and never names a single code below threshold. For classification it returns a ranked candidate set with per-candidate CROSS citations and calibrated confidence, and below threshold it shows the two or three live candidates, the duty spread between them, the rulings that separate them, and marks the SKU "unresolved, do not file on this alone." For scope it renders a "contested scope" card containing the order's scope paragraph verbatim, the two nearest scope rulings with their holdings and citations, a similarity score, and the concrete next observable — the pending scope-ruling docket and its statutory deadline — then downgrades the account's exposure from a point estimate to a labelled range with the unresolved tuple broken out, and auto-subscribes the user to that docket so the ambiguity resolves itself when Commerce rules. Where an exporter-specific rate cannot be matched to a supplier name it falls back to the all-others rate and labels it "exporter unmatched — all-others rate applied, upper bound." More than 20% of an uploaded catalog unresolved auto-refunds the month in-product. There is no broker queue and no "ask our trade expert" button — the stated boundary is monitoring and evidence assembly, explicitly not customs advice or entry filing. A4: every source is machine-readable and was verified live — the USITC HTS reststop returns the schedule as JSON with htsno, indent, description, general/special/other rates, units, footnotes and additionalDuties per line; CBP CROSS returns JSON ruling objects carrying rulingNumber, tariffs, rulingDate and, critically, revokedBy/revokes/modifiedBy/modifies, so precedent staleness is a field in the data rather than a guess; and the Federal Register API returned 10,000 tariff-matching documents with the newest published 2026-08-12. Add CSMS entry-filing instructions, the CBP AD/CVD case list with exporter-specific rates and effective periods, USTR exclusion expiry mapped to Chapter 99, and the ITC sunset calendar. A5: nightly ingest with weekly full reindex and known-answer canary SKUs run after every corpus refresh — a failed canary blocks promotion of the new index and freezes alerting rather than emitting wrong rates; HTS unrefreshed in 48h or CROSS in 7 days banners "rates as of <date>, unverified" and suppresses new classification assertions; a business day with zero matched Federal Register documents or an unparseable HTS revision string halts alerting and marks every exposure figure "as of <last good timestamp>." A6: zero human minutes — every alert carries its own primary-source citation and effective date, and an in-app "why this code" evidence trace answers the modal question.

name: Redlist
one_liner: Watches the two enforcement systems that stop consumer goods at the door — California Prop 65 60-day notices and FDA import alert red lists — against your own catalog and supplier list, and shows the wave 30–90 days before it reaches your SKU.
summary: JTBD (Christensen): "tell me my product category or my supplier is being worked, before the demand letter or the frantic port call." Both halves are one-directional information asymmetries hitting the same buyer. Prop 65 is enforced by private bounty-hunter plaintiffs filing roughly 316–593 notices a month through 2025 (Sep 520, Oct 593 — 4,500–5,000 a year and rising), who systematically work product categories (drinkware, vinyl bags, cookware, supplements, cosmetics); an attorney-negotiated settlement runs $10,000–$20,000 inside the 60-day window and $40,000–$90,000 once suit is filed. FDA Detention Without Physical Examination is a paper detention: once a firm, product, or country-and-product-code pair lands on an import alert, "every shipment tied to it gets hit with DWPE... and FDA skips the inspection entirely," discovered as a frantic call when customs will not release; demurrage at ~$200/container/day means a modest 10-day delay across a 12-container sailing is $24,000 unplanned on one shipment, the detention notice carries a hard 10-working-day deadline, and getting off an alert takes months to over a year. Beachhead (Moore): 7–8 figure Amazon/Shopify sellers and consumer brands with 100–5,000 SKUs shipping into California from Asia, LatAm and the EU — the same person owns the catalog and the supplier list, which is why these two corpora belong in one product rather than two. WTP (Hormozi): $199 one-time category report and $99–$599/mo, framed as "see the wave before it reaches your SKU" and priced at 1–2% of a single $20k settlement or ~1.5% of one avoided 12-container DWPE event. Moat (Helmer — assembly, not access): the California AG 60-day notice database is searchable from 1988 to present but exposes no CSV export, no bulk download and no API, so a clean structured mirror with full history is a genuine cornered resource; the crown jewels are the AG settlement PDFs, parsed into the only structured table of what concentration actually settles by category and chemical, since the negotiated reformulation ppm limits that define de facto compliance live only inside those PDFs. On the FDA side the asset is entity resolution — matching a customer's supplier, with its transliterated name variants, trade names, shared addresses and sister facilities, to FDA's own inconsistent firm strings — plus a retained add/remove timeline answering "when did this firm go on and come off," which is the defensible remainder even if FDA someday ships a subscribe-by-firm feed. Bullseye (Weinberg & Mares): free public notice search with defendant, plaintiff and category pages, and free per-alert and per-country/product-code pages — people search their own company name and "Prop 65 60-day notice" the day the letter arrives, and brokers search alert numbers constantly. Known weakness to design against: purchase is trigger-driven, which is excellent for the one-time report and hostile to subscription retention, so the daily category feed and the pre-shipment green-light check must carry renewal.
autonomy_case: A1: email plus Stripe; the $199 category report and the $99 supplier screen are paste-or-upload-and-pay flows delivered before any account exists, and subscriptions upgrade and cancel in-app. Onboarding is picking categories from a list our own corpus generated, or dropping a catalog or supplier CSV. A2: threat scores, plaintiff-firm dossiers, the ppm reformulation table, the daily notice digest, the alert-history timeline and the safe-harbor warning text (a template fill from the OEHHA chemical name in the regulation-specified format, not drafting) are all generated — no human review, no queue. A3: a false all-clear is the one output that could cause real harm, so the product never renders an affirmative "you are clear" — it renders "no matched alert entries as of <timestamp>, monitoring N of M suppliers resolved." When category matching is weak it refuses to emit a threat score at all: it prints "no close precedent — 4 loose matches at 0.41 similarity," shows those four notices verbatim with AG numbers and dates, and drops the user into a raw keyword-filtered feed. A settlement PDF yielding no extractable ppm renders "limit not stated in settlement" with a link to the source page rather than an inferred number. A fuzzy supplier match below threshold emits a "possible match — 0.78" card with the customer's record and the FDA firm record side by side and differing fields highlighted, plus one-click confirm or dismiss on the customer's own data; if they do nothing the tuple stays unconfirmed and is excluded from any clear status. Total entity-resolution failure degrades the account to country plus product-code monitoring and says so explicitly on the dashboard rather than showing green. Every claim carries its primary-source URL and notice date; a month producing only unresolved cards auto-issues a prorated credit. There is no expert path and no attorney referral — the stated boundary is that it reports what has been filed and settled, and never opines on liability or admissibility. A4: 03:00 PT daily paginated delta scrape of the notice DB keyed on AG number, Sunday settlement-PDF harvest and extraction, 05:00 ET daily crawl of the FDA alerts-by-publish-date index with every changed alert page diffed at firm-entry level, openFDA enforcement and warning-letter endpoints daily, OEHHA list checked daily for revision date, monthly refusal reports, CPSC hourly, ECHA SVHC monthly. A5: the liveness signals are genuine rather than timestamps. The notice DB is expected to gain rows every business day, so three consecutive business days with zero new AG numbers trips the watchdog and halts threat-score rendering. A maximum alert publish date that has not advanced in 7 days, or a per-alert parsed firm count swinging more than 15% (a layout break), fails closed, freezes alerting, and shows a dated last-verified banner rather than implying all-clear. A parse-rate drop on the settlement extractor blocks publication of that batch rather than shipping garbage. A6: zero human minutes — the two predictable questions ("what is this notice" and "does this apply to me") are the product's own screens, and the confirm/dismiss UI absorbs the rest.

name: Allowed Amount
one_liner: Joins the reimbursement benchmarks payers and CMS are legally required to publish — MRF negotiated rates, weekly coverage and NCCI edits, weekly NADAC — to a provider's own NPI and code mix, and alerts the month one of them moves.
summary: JTBD (Christensen): "tell me my money changed before the revenue sags." Three public corpora answer three questions no small provider can answer today. What a payer has published it agreed to pay you: since 2022 every payer must publish machine-readable in-network files monthly, and the CMS schema explicitly carries provider_groups with an npi array and a tin object alongside negotiated_rate, negotiated_type, billing_code_modifier and service_code — so the answer to "what did this payer agree to pay me for 99214?" is already public and completely inaccessible, because Cigna itself warns the files may be "as large as one Terabyte" and are "not intended to be opened on personal workstations." What CMS just changed that will start denying you: the Medicare Coverage Database ships weekly on Thursdays and NCCI PTP/MUE republish quarterly with individual files running to 475,091 records in the 2026 Q3 release; an MUE denial is a coding denial, so the practice cannot bill the patient either and the loss is total and silent — discovered six weeks later in an EOB pile. And where you were reimbursed below acquisition cost: NADAC refreshes weekly on data.medicaid.gov (verified modified 2026-08-11) and is exactly what Colorado's 1 Jan 2026 PBM floor and New Jersey's commercial floor key on, yet practitioners report most pharmacies have never executed the statutory appeal because the detection step is missing. Beachhead (Moore): 5 payers × 3 metros × the top 200 codes, sold into 1–15 provider practices with high code concentration and thin margins where one edit moves real money — PT/OT, behavioral health, dermatology, sleep, wound care, allergy, imaging. Channel: the small billing companies and RCM shops that serve them, because one arrives with dozens of NPIs and resells white-labelled digests — which is also the answer to healthcare's slow buying, since practices defer to their biller anyway. WTP (Ramanujam): a single silently-amended E/M rate across a 4,000-visit year is a five-figure annual swing, and $149–$399/mo sits below the level where a practice manager needs physician-owner sign-off, which is what makes genuine self-serve conversion possible in a segment famous for sales-assisted buying. Moat (Helmer, cornered resource): payers overwrite their files rather than archive them, so a monthly historical series answering "what was your rate every month for two years" is unreconstructable by a later entrant; and CMS publishes snapshots, not changelogs, so the longitudinal diff answering "what changed in this document, in this edit pair, in this MUE value, and when did it take effect" is assembly nobody sells to small practices. The firms that solved MRF ingestion (Turquoise, Serif — billions of rows a month, 200+ payers) sell enterprise contracts with no published price, and a self-serve SMB tier would cannibalise them: the classic incumbent disincentive. Bullseye: a free "what does <payer> publish for your NPI on 99213?" lookup with NPPES autocomplete, plus a free weekly "what changed in this Thursday's drop" digest and per-code change-history pages. Two hard constraints to settle before writing code: CPT descriptors are AMA-licensed IP, so the product must be built on CMS-published HCPCS, code numbers and customer-supplied code lists without redistributing descriptor text; and the parser must reject anything patient-identifying, keeping the core product out of HIPAA scope by design.
autonomy_case: A1: type a practice name, pick the NPI from NPPES autocomplete, Stripe Checkout, report renders — and because no PHI touches the core product there is no BAA negotiation, no security questionnaire and no call, so the usual healthcare sales friction is designed out of the product rather than sold through. The $149 quarterly impact report needs nothing but an email and a two-column CSV. A2: streaming ingest, indexing, diffing, benchmarking, personalisation against the customer's code list and volumes, the dollar math against their MAC's fee schedule, and alerting are all code. A3: MRF data quality is genuinely poor and CRS has published a whole report on it, so the engine never guesses. A code with no matching record shows "not published by this payer for your TIN as of <file date>" with a link to the source file and record location. Where negotiated_type is "percentage" or "derived" the row is labelled and NOT converted into a dollar figure. Conflicting records for the same tuple are all shown with their plan identifiers instead of the engine picking a winner, and market-percentile benchmarks are suppressed entirely below a minimum n. On the CMS side jurisdiction ambiguity is never collapsed — both readings render side by side with both dollar figures ("applies only if your MAC is Noridian JE and POS is 11"), the item is labelled "unresolved — 2 readings," the governing paragraph is quoted verbatim with document ID and version date, unresolved items are excluded from headline totals, and the user can set the disambiguating fact once in settings so it resolves permanently. It never asserts a modifier is "clinically appropriate" — that is a clinical judgement and the product says so and links the CMS text. An NDC absent from that week's NADAC file returns "no published benchmark for this NDC in the week of <date> — not evaluated," never an inferred gap, and where the PBM contract rate rather than the statutory floor governs it names which claims it cannot judge. Appeal and dispute documents are generated for the provider to file through the payer's own portal; the product never files, appeals, negotiates or represents anyone, and there is no coder queue or consult upsell. An optional paid-versus-published check runs the practice's 835/ERA file entirely client-side so PHI never reaches our servers. A4: monthly MRF refresh is regulatorily mandated, so a payer whose file has not updated in more than 40 days is flagged stale in-product rather than silently aging; MCD downloads and diffs every Thursday with a daily Coverage API poll for out-of-band NCD activity; NCCI polled daily in the two weeks around each 1 Jan/Apr/Jul/Oct effective date; NADAC weekly; NPPES weekly; MPFS/GPCI quarterly; and the CMSgov price-transparency-guide schema versions are tracked so parsers do not silently break on a schema bump. A5: hash and record-count validation gates everything — an MCD file hash unchanged across two consecutive Thursdays, or a quarterly NCCI file more than 10% off the prior quarter's record count, fails closed and suppresses that source's alerts behind a dated staleness banner; a NADAC file more than 10 days old hard-blocks new underwater findings rather than comparing a fill against a superseded week; schema-version regression tests gate deploys and hard per-payer cost ceilings fail closed on the terabyte-scale ingest. A6: zero human minutes — every alert carries the primary source document and the diff that produced it.
